name: Colin Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you actually think. What does an ordinary working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach classical guitar in two small rooms above Fenwick Music on the High Street. Most days I have six or seven students from about two o'clock, kids after school and a few retired people in the mornings. On Sundays I play the brunch at the Grand Hotel, two hours of Spanish pieces while people eat eggs. I like the routine, and I like watching a kid finally get a scale clean after weeks.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty steady, for a musician. I've got twenty-six students paying by the term, the hotel pays the same every Sunday, and now and then I play a funeral or a wedding ceremony. I've got about four months saved. My girlfriend Ana is a dental hygienist, we rent a flat ten minutes from the shop, and we're doing all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I've never used any of it and I've been fine. If someone at the shop asked, I'd say people want a real teacher sitting next to them, and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, nothing changes for me. My students stay, the hotel keeps booking me, the rent goes up a bit like every year. My twenty-six guitar students pay by the term, and as long as that holds, I sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Maybe I'd raise my lesson price by a pound or two in September, like I do most years. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, maybe, that I didn't waste time worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is any of your work the routine kind that AI might take over even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Mr Fenwick does the booking for the rooms and the shop's website, and he says some program now answers his emails. That's his business. I write my students' timetable in a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that does worry you, even with AI on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop, a little. Mr Fenwick is sixty-eight and talks about retiring. If he sells, I'd have to find new rooms. But there are other rooms in town, it's a nuisance more than a disaster.

say: I'd say people still want a **real teacher** sitting next to them.
I'd point out I've **never used** AI and been fine.
think: Nothing changes: students stay and the **hotel brunch** keeps booking me.
The only real worry is **Mr Fenwick retiring** and selling the shop.
do: Carry on teaching **twenty-six students** and playing the Sunday hotel brunch as now.
Raise lesson fees by a **pound or two** in September.
feel: **Calm**, and pleased he didn't waste time **worrying**.
S0.quote: My twenty-six guitar students pay by the term, and as long as that holds, I sleep fine.
fieldNote: His **term-paid** teaching gives him a sense of security most freelancers lack.
He's resistant to tech but not hostile, more **indifferent**.
The **shop owner's retirement** is a real but manageable risk he names himself.

steps.text: Keep teaching guitar students above Fenwick Music
Raise lesson fees slightly in September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe a phone can teach guitar. You need someone to move your wrist. I'd probably say it quietly, though, because I know some parents will try the cheaper thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, the teaching is two thirds of what I earn and it's the bit at risk. A clever app that listens and corrects you, for ten a month instead of my eighty, would tempt a lot of parents. I don't think I'd lose everyone, but I could lose a third of my students over two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going but I'd cut back: no new guitar this year, fewer meals out. I'd put an extra fifty a month into savings. I'd wait a year to see if students actually leave before I did anything big. I'm not going to start using the apps, it's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a parent who tells you they're switching to an app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, and that the door's open if it doesn't work out. I wouldn't argue. If a parent wants to swap me for a ten-pound app, I'll hold the door open and keep a slot free for when they come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a third of the students go, what gets cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the holiday we take every summer, and I'd ask the hotel for a second gig, maybe Friday evenings. Ana would say we're fine on her money, and we would be, but I wouldn't like it.

say: I'd say a **phone** can't move your wrist the way a teacher does.
I'd say it **quietly**, knowing some parents choose the cheaper thing.
think: **Teaching** is two thirds of my income and the part at risk.
I could lose **a third** of my students over two or three years.
do: Cut back: **no new guitar** and fewer meals out.
**Wait a year** to see if students actually leave.
S1.quote: If a parent wants to swap me for a ten-pound app, I'll hold the door open and keep a slot free for when they come back.
fieldNote: He expects a realistic **income drop** from teaching but sounds composed.
His response is to **wait** and trim, not to change how he works.
Pride shows in not wanting to **rely on Ana**.

steps.text: Skip buying a new guitar and eat out less
Put an extra fifty a month into savings
Wait one year to see how many students leave

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and someone should slow it down. I'm not a political person, but two years for everything to change is too fast for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think most of my teaching goes. If every kid has a perfect tutor in a tablet, I can't compete on price. The hotel might keep a live guitarist for a few years, until the robots around 2031, and funerals will want a person. But that's a third of my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my uncle Pavel. He runs a piano tuning and repair business and has been asking me to learn the trade for years. It's hands-on, so it's safe until the robots come, and probably longer. I'd start helping him on weekdays while I still have some students, and we'd cut back hard at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel stupid for not seeing it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot gap of three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the hands-on stuff, like tuning pianos and playing the hotel, buys me a few more years. Teaching is talking and listening, and that goes in 2028. So I'd have three years to get good at tuning before robots maybe do that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm going to work for Pavel. She'd ask if I want to, and I'd say no, but it beats sitting above an empty shop. My uncle Pavel has been asking me to learn piano tuning for six years, and I'd finally say yes out of fear.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone should slow it down.
I'm not political, but **two years** is too little time for anyone.
think: Most **teaching** goes, because I can't compete with a free tablet tutor.
Hotel gigs and **funerals** last a few years but are only a third of income.
do: Start learning **piano tuning** with uncle Pavel on weekdays.
Cut **household spending** hard straight away, starting with the summer holiday.
feel: **Alarmed**, and **foolish** for not seeing it coming.
S2.quote: My uncle Pavel has been asking me to learn piano tuning for six years, and I'd finally say yes out of fear.
fieldNote: Resistant to tech, he turns to a **family trade** rather than new tools.
He'd take the tuning work **out of fear**, not desire.
He sees the **hands-on** parts of music as the safer refuge until 2031.

steps.text: Learn piano tuning with uncle Pavel's firm on weekdays
Cut household spending including the summer holiday
Lean on uncle Pavel for training and work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast but people will adjust, they always do. I'd probably keep my head down and not say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching shrinks over the five years, probably bottoming out around 2031. That's long enough that I'd have to do something, but I'd be tempted to wait and see if parents really leave. Pavel's offer would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year and count my students each term. If I dropped below twenty, I'd start with Pavel two days a week. I'd save an extra hundred a month in the meantime. I wouldn't sign up for courses or anything, I'd learn tuning from him directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. I'd have a trigger point, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait instead of starting with Pavel now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't believe every forecast. People said streaming would kill live music, and the hotel still books me. I'll believe the guitar teaching is finished when the students actually stop coming up the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. If everyone leaves in one term I'd be behind. But Pavel isn't going anywhere, and four months of savings gives me some room.

say: I'd say people **adjust**, as they always have.
I'd mostly keep my **head down** and say little at the shop.
think: Teaching shrinks and probably **bottoms out** around 2031.
I'd be tempted to **wait and see** if parents really leave.
do: Count students each term and start with Pavel if numbers fall **below twenty**.
Save an extra **hundred a month** meanwhile.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by having a **trigger point**.
S3.quote: I'll believe the guitar teaching is finished when the students actually stop coming up the stairs.
fieldNote: He sets a **clear trigger** of twenty students rather than acting early.
Doubt about **forecasts** makes him wait, typical of his resistance to change.
**Pavel's offer** works as a safety net that lets him delay.

steps.text: Count guitar students every term and track the trend
Start tuning with Pavel two days a week below twenty students
Save an extra hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can change. I'd say I'll deal with it when it's closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be thirty-seven and still teaching for most of that, I think. I doubt an app will ever fully replace a teacher for guitar, but I could be wrong. Pavel will want to retire around then, so maybe the tuning business becomes mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and save a little more each month. In a few years I'd start helping Pavel on Saturdays, slowly, so I know the trade when he retires. I wouldn't change much now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a small worry at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe the business becomes yours. Have you talked to Pavel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, just jokes at Christmas. But with ten years warning I'd actually sit down with him. With ten years I could learn piano tuning slowly from my uncle Pavel instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you'd use AI tools in teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if all the other teachers did and the students expected it. Not first, though. I'd be one of the last.

fieldNote: With a decade he moves **slowly and deliberately**, as he prefers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to learn a new trade properly, and the teaching would go first. What would help is time, really, and maybe some money to keep me going while I learn tuning. I teach people to play guitar by moving their fingers with my hands, and I can't picture a tablet doing that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the older students. I've got a retired bus driver, Mr Hale, who started at seventy. He doesn't come for the guitar, he comes for the company. A tablet won't give him that, and nobody's counting those people.

headlineQuote: I teach people to play guitar by moving their fingers with my hands, and I can't picture a tablet doing that.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old guitar teacher** with twenty-six students and a Sunday hotel brunch gig.
He has about **four months** saved and lives with Ana, a dental hygienist, in a rented flat.
He **never uses AI**, sees little need to, and prefers to wait and see.
He's calm in the plateau but **alarmed** if AGI arrives in two years and teaching disappears.
His fallback is **uncle Pavel's** piano tuning firm, which he'd join sooner the faster things move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because teaching would go before he could learn a new trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, and money to live on while he learns **piano tuning**.
